Chapter 2: The Power of Comparisons and the Trap of Anchoring
Every day, we're faced with choices—some feel trivial, while others could change everything. But here's the thing: the way we make those choices isn't always as straightforward as we'd like to think. More often than not, our decisions are shaped by comparisons, even when those comparisons are completely random or misleading.
Picture this: you're out shopping for a new TV. You walk into the store, determined to find the best value. On display are three options—a basic model, a mid-range one, and then a fancy top-of-the-line version loaded with features most of us would never use. Now, that expensive model? It's not really there to be sold. It's there to make the mid-range TV look like a steal.
Faced with these choices, most people end up picking the one in the middle, feeling smart and balanced. But this setup isn’t a coincidence. Retailers and marketers know that we rarely evaluate things all by themselves. Instead, we lean on relative comparisons. Just the presence of a “decoy” option—something obviously overpriced or lacking—can nudge us toward a particular choice. It's not the absolute value that pulls us in, but how it stacks up against what's right next to it.
And it's not just shopping. Think about job offers. You might be less focused on the actual salary, and more on how it compares to what your friends are making. Or maybe you're house hunting with your partner. After seeing a slightly pricier house, you stretch your budget, convinced you're landing a better deal by comparison.
Then there's anchoring—a force that's just as powerful. In one experiment, people were asked if the tallest redwood tree was more or less than 1,200 feet tall—a number chosen at random. Then, they had to guess the tree’s real height. Those who heard the high anchor gave much higher guesses than those who heard a smaller number. That first figure, even though it made no sense, set the stage for all the thinking that came after.
This isn’t just about trivia games. Car salespeople do it all the time, kicking off negotiations with a steep sticker price. Every counteroffer you make gets weighed against that anchor. And even in our personal lives, first impressions can serve as anchors—shaping how we see someone long after the first hello.
Our minds use comparisons and anchors to help us make quick decisions in a world that’s pretty complicated. That can be a real strength. But it also opens us up to mistakes and even manipulation. Most of us don’t realize just how much the way options are presented can sway our choices.
Here’s a great example: a magazine once offered three subscription options. Online-only, print-only, and then a combined print-and-online package for the exact same price as print-only. No one picked the print-only choice—it was just there as a decoy. But its presence made the combined offer look like an absolute bargain. When they took away the decoy, far fewer people chose the combined option.
These patterns show up everywhere—in big decisions and small ones. So, what’s the key takeaway?
Context matters. Our minds are wired to compare, to anchor, and to see value in relation to what’s nearby. Noticing this habit is the first step toward making choices that genuinely fit your own values and needs.
